The two gates

Gate 1 — Sign

Signing freezes a cut into a TEP. The gate refuses:

  • an empty cut;

  • a change with no acceptance criteria ("nothing proves this");

  • a change with no grounding (no place in the code);

  • an ask in the cut with an undecided question;

  • a cut that neither lands documentation nor carries a recorded exemption — documentation is required for every cut at signing, and the only way past it is an exemption with a reason.

The click mints TEP-<you>-<n> and a machine-local HMAC token bound to the pair you actually saw: the rendered cut screen plus the grounded content underneath it — the documentation decision included. There is no expiry — instead, any edit to the signed content makes the token stop matching, and dispatch refuses until you sign again. What runs is exactly what you approved, enforced cryptographically rather than by convention.

Gate 2 — Accept

A delivery page opens by naming the run that produced it and when — or says plainly that the run was never recorded, for an old delivery that predates the field — before any other section. It then names every acceptance criterion of the cut with its verdict: green, red, "for you to certify" for what only the running product can show, or "not checked" for a criterion nothing judged — a criterion is never left off the page for want of a proof that mentions it. Proofs that answer no single criterion, such as the repository’s own test suite or a red push, are listed beside the criteria rather than folded into them. The pull request the gate opens carries that same complete list, so the delivery page and the pull request never say different things about a criterion. Accepting:

  • is refused for a delivery that was withheld, or one with no proof at all;

  • is refused while any acceptance criterion of the cut is red — an unkept promise is the one thing that is never handed over;

  • is refused while a declared documentation obligation is unmet (the docs gate blocks by default; thinkubeTandem.docsGateMode: advisory is the recorded escape hatch for a documentation obligation that slipped through to a delivery — documentation itself is already required at signing, with a recorded exemption as the only way past it there);

  • runs in the canonical order merge → stamp → retire: a refused merge aborts before anything is stamped; worktree cleanup is best-effort and never fails a landed accept.

Everything that did NOT arrive is printed on the page — UNDELIVERED items, confessions found by the honesty scan, unmet obligations. Red is shown as red; there is no override on a red promise.

Findings — what the machine could not settle

Not every red thing is a veto. A delivery also carries findings: things the machine noticed, could not settle, and has no actor left to route to — a standing test that stayed red after every repairer was spent, a review that disagreed, a size or reachability opinion, production code that imitates the editor platform.

These get their own section on the delivery page and they do not block Accept. That is deliberate. A rule may veto only when its failure names somebody who can still act; by the time you are reading the page, that somebody is you. Holding four kept promises hostage to a hygiene opinion nobody can act on serves nobody — so the machine says what it saw, in full, and the judgement is yours.

Two things still veto, and only two: an unkept promise, and a product that does not build. The second is not a matter of taste — handing over something that cannot ship harms whoever pulls it, whatever you decide.

Observations — what only the running product can show

Some acceptance criteria cannot be driven by any check: they are about what the product looks like or feels like when it runs. These are recorded as observations rather than graded green, listed on the delivery, and left for you to confirm by using the thing. The machine never marks an observation proven on its own account.
